As a matter of policy, the Treasury has never disclosed Saudi Arabia's holdings, though the kingdom has long been a key ally in the volatile Middle East, and instead lumps it together with 14 other mostly OPEC nations including Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Nigeria.

title: Anna Deavere Smith turns the lens on her own story
text: Anna Deavere Smith is coming home. The protean actress and playwright has built her career on interviewing and then embodying people of different races and contrasting points of view — “chasing that which is not me,” as she described it in a recent interview. Her new play, “Notes From the Field,” an extended meditation on education and criminal justice, is different. “This piece,” she said, “is about me.” The audience may not see that right away. Like her earlier work, including her best-known plays, “Fires in the Mirror,” about the 1991 race riots in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, and “Twilight: Los Angeles, 1992,” about the Rodney King riots, “Notes From the Field” is built on scores of interviews. Ms. Smith plays 19 characters, among them Linda Wayman, the committed principal of a struggling high school in Philadelphia; Kevin Moore, the deli worker in Baltimore who videotaped police officers dragging Freddie Gray into a police transport van; and Niya Kenny, the high school student in Columbia, S.C., who videotaped a sheriff's deputy slamming a girl to the floor while trying to remove her from her desk. As in her other plays, these people appear in their own words, with Ms. Smith reproducing their intonation and cadence. But the themes of “Notes From the Field” are unusually personal, she said in an interview in Cambridge, Mass., in late August. Her mother was a teacher and later a principal in the Baltimore public school system; many aunts and family friends were teachers as well. All of these women believed deeply in the power of education to lift children out of poverty. Yet her interviews revealed a system that in most cases no longer seemed able to do that.

title: Supreme Court seems unlikely to revive Obama immigration plan
text: President Barack Obama's effort to rescue his plan to shield millions of immigrants living in the country illegally from deportation and give them work permits ran into difficulty at the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, in a case testing the limits of presidential power. The court, which has four conservative and four liberal justices, appeared split along ideological lines during 90 minutes of arguments in the case brought by 26 states led by Texas, which sued to block Obama's unilateral 2014 executive action that bypassed Congress. The liberal justices voiced support for Obama's action, while the conservatives sounded skeptical. A 4-4 ruling would be a grim defeat for Obama, because it would leave in place lower court rulings that struck down his action last year and doom his effort to overhaul a U.S. immigration policy he calls broken. More than a thousand supporters of Obama's action held a raucous demonstration outside the white marble courthouse on a sunny spring day, as cheerful mariachi music from a band dressed in red and black filled the air. A smaller group of Obama critics held its own rally. To win, Obama would need the support of one of the court's conservatives, most likely Chief Justice John Roberts or Anthony Kennedy. But both at times pressed the Obama administration's lawyer, U.S. Solicitor General Donald Verrilli, with tough questions. Kennedy voiced concern that Obama had exceeded his authority by having the executive branch set immigration policy instead of carrying out laws passed by Congress. “It's as if the president is setting the policy and the Congress is executing it. That's just upside down,” Kennedy said. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

title: Obama moves to ease terrorism fears before the holidays
text: President Obama will visit the Pentagon and the National Counterterrorism Center this week, in visits meant to reassure the nation about the White House strategy for fighting terrorism. Obama addressed the nation from the Oval Office at the White House in Washington on Dec. 6. Fears of terrorism are hanging over America's holiday season, and Obama has planned a series of events this week aimed at calming concerns about his strategy for stopping the Islamic State group abroad and its sympathizers at home. To ease fears about terrorism, President Obama will devote much of the coming week to discussing his strategies for countering the influence of the Islamic State (IS) militant group at home and abroad. In recent weeks, the president has struck an increasingly soothing tone in response to the terrorist attacks in Paris and San Bernardino, Calif., urging Americans not to let distrust and fear pull them apart. "Terrorists like ISIL are trying to divide us along lines of religion and background," Obama said in his weekly address on Sunday, using an acronym for the extremist group. "That's how they stoke fear. That's how they recruit." Yet for a growing number of Americans, those fears are very real in the wake of the terrorist attacks in Paris and San Bernardino, Calif. In January, a Press-GfK poll found that 5 in 10 Americans believed the risk of a terrorist attack in the United States was high. title: Trump takes aim at Toyota over Mexico, but Nissan has more to lose
text: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump has threatened Toyota Motor Corp (7203.T) over its Mexican-built cars, but a punitive tariff would pose the biggest risk to its compatriot Nissan Motor Co (7201.T), the largest automaker operating in Mexico. On Thursday he turned on Toyota, warning the world's largest automaker that it would face a “big border tax” if it exported Mexico-built cars to the U.S. market. But Nissan, Japan's second-largest automaker, would be the bigger casualty of any tax penalty. Nissan built its first overseas plant in Mexico 50 years ago and now makes more than 800,000 cars there, mostly its entry-level Versa and Sentra sedans. Mexican-made vehicles account for roughly one-quarter of Nissan's total U.S. vehicle sales, industry experts say, compared with around 30 percent for its smaller rival Mazda and less than 10 percent for Toyota and Honda. title: Trump team blocks Pentagon nominee's House appearance, officials say
text: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump's team has called off an appearance before Congress by his choice for defense secretary, retired General James Mattis, concerning a waiver he needs to take the job, congressional officials said on Wednesday. The U.S. House of Representatives had been scheduled to hear testimony from Mattis on Thursday, and he had agreed to appear. Mattis, who retired from the Marine Corps in 2013, is technically ineligible to serve as defense secretary because he has not been a civilian for at least seven years. Congress would therefore have to grant a waiver, which it has not done since 1950. House Democratic Whip Steny Hoyer said he understood that the Trump transition team had blocked Mattis from testifying. Congressional aides also confirmed that Mattis had agreed to testify but that the appearance had been blocked. The move appeared to be part of an effort to keep the focus on Mattis' Senate confirmation hearing, which is set for earlier on Thursday. “This (waiver) is not a minor issue. This is a major issue affecting the principle of civilian control of the military, and Ranking Member (Representative Adam) Smith believes deeply that General Mattis should come speak with the members about it,” said Barron Youngsmith, a spokesman for Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee. A Trump transition team spokeswoman did not address the House hearing directly but said Mattis was currently focused on the Senate confirmation process and “testifying at his confirmation hearing of the Senate Armed Services Committee.” “If confirmed he looks forward to working with both the Senate and House Armed Services Committees, which play critical roles in supporting our forces and ensuring civilian control of the military,” Alleigh Marre said in a statement.

title: Suspected U.S. drone strike on Haqqani militants in Pakistan kills four
text: A suspected U.S. drone strike on Thursday hit a hideout of the Haqqani militant network on Pakistan's mountainous border with Afghanistan, killing four people, officials said. If confirmed, it would be the fourth such U.S. strike inside Pakistan since President Donald Trump took office in January. Two Pakistani intelligence officials and a local government officer said an unmanned aerial vehicle fired two missiles at a compound housing militants commanded by a senior network commander, Abdur Rasheed Haqqani. Villagers first reported a blast in the Upper Kurram area to the authorities, one of the officials said, adding: "We got it from our informant later that it was a U.S. drone strike that targeted Haqqanis." It was unclear whether the commander was among the dead, said the officials, who asked not to be named because the issue is sensitive. Trump's new strategy for the war in Afghanistan calls for a tougher line with Pakistan on militants such as the Haqqani network who have bases inside Pakistan. Since the Afghan policy review, the U.S. has been pressing Islamabad for decisive action against the Haqqani network militants, who are notorious for using Pakistani soil to launch attacks on American-led NATO troops in Afghanistan. Islamabad denies the allegations and instead blames Kabul for failing to eliminate militants who use Afghan territory as a base for attacks on targets in Pakistan. Pakistan has been battling a deadly Islamist militancy for more than a decade. On Wednesday, gunmen attacked a minority Shi'ite Muslim mosque in Islamabad, the capital, killing two people. Lashkar-e-Jhangvi al-Alami, a Sunni sectarian group linked to the militant group Islamic State, claimed responsibility for the mosque attack.
